result: The authors developed and validated a longitudinal in vivo imaging method to track single motor units in the Tibialis anterior muscle of SOD1G37R/YFP mice over multiple sessions. In wild-type mice, all NMJs remained stably innervated across all imaging sessions (36/36 NMJs, 5/5 motor units), demonstrating the reliability of the method.
evaluation: Claims C13-C21 establish a robust methodology for longitudinal imaging of motor units. The validation in wild-type mice (C19-C21) demonstrates technical reliability with 100% stability of NMJs over time, consistent with prior literature. The method is well-documented with appropriate controls and sample sizes.

result: SOD1G37R/YFP mice were phenotypically and histologically indistinguishable from SOD1G37R mice, demonstrating that YFP expression does not alter disease progression or increase motor neuron susceptibility to ALS pathology.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24 provide essential validation that the YFP reporter does not confound the disease model. This is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing comparable body weight, grip strength, motor neuron counts, and NMJ denervation between SOD1G37R and SOD1G37R/YFP mice.

result: In SOD1G37R/YFP mice, motor units lost NMJs asynchronously over multiple imaging sessions rather than abruptly. YFP-labeled nerve terminals gradually retracted from some postsynaptic sites (partial losses: 29/253 NMJs; complete losses: 38/253 NMJs across 16/19 motor unit arbors) while other branches remained innervated, indicating that NMJ loss occurs as a slow, branch-specific process independent of global axonal degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C25-C31 present the core finding of asynchronous NMJ loss. The quantitative data (29 partial and 38 complete losses across 253 NMJs) and longitudinal imaging evidence strongly support this conclusion. The observation that some branches remain innervated while others degenerate within the same motor unit directly demonstrates asynchronous, branch-specific denervation.

result: A subset of motor axons eventually underwent synchronous degeneration where all remaining NMJs were lost simultaneously (7/19 motor unit arbors). Importantly, signs of asynchronous NMJ denervation preceded most synchronous motor unit degenerations (6/7 arbors), often by more than a month (≥3 sessions in 11/19 arbors), revealing two distinct phases: initial slow branch-specific dismantlement followed by sudden global axonal degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 identify the biphasic pattern of motor unit degeneration. The quantitative data (7/19 arbors with synchronous loss, 6/7 preceded by asynchronous changes) and temporal analysis (≥3 sessions = >1 month) are well-documented. The interpretation that synchronous loss reflects motor neuron death (C33) is reasonable speculation supported by the data pattern.

result: Fiber type analysis revealed that nearly all superficial fibers in the imaged region were fast-fatigable (myosin heavy-chain type IIb or IIx), indicating that different patterns of motor unit degeneration observed are unlikely due to differences in motor unit types.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 address a potential confounding variable. The fiber typing data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) demonstrates homogeneity of motor unit types in the imaged region, strengthening the conclusion that observed variability in degeneration patterns reflects disease mechanisms rather than motor unit type differences.

result: A vast majority of motor units (14/19 arbors, 9/11 animals) sprouted toward nearby postsynaptic sites, forming new synaptic contacts (76/253 NMJs). These motor unit expansions resulted in a net increase in motor unit size (80.7±32.2% expansions vs 26.0±10.2% losses at session 6), masking contemporaneous NMJ dismantlement. Over half of motor units (13/19 arbors) both lost and formed new NMJs, demonstrating that these opposite processes can occur simultaneously within a single motor unit.
evaluation: Claims C39-C42 reveal the dynamic compensatory response. The quantitative data showing extensive motor unit expansions (76/253 NMJs) occurring simultaneously with losses in the same motor units (13/19 arbors) is well-documented and supported by imaging evidence. This finding reconciles the 'dying-back hypothesis' with observed motor unit enlargement.

result: There was an inverse relationship between the propensity of axonal branches to be lost versus to expand. Distal branches were more susceptible to loss (logistic regression, p=0.010) while proximal branches (mainly first-order) were more likely to expand (logistic regression, p=0.001), indicating that proximal branches preserve their capacity to reinnervate heterologous NMJs despite ongoing distal degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C43-C46 identify spatial patterns in motor unit dynamics. The statistical analysis (logistic regression with p=0.010 and p=0.001) provides strong quantitative support. The sample size (253 NMJs, 19 arbors, 11 animals) is adequate, and the finding is consistent with energetic load hypotheses of neurodegeneration.

result: Despite extensive motor unit expansions, few motor units re-innervated their own lost NMJs (autologous re-innervation: 2/21 possibilities) and most partial losses were not repaired (15/40 possibilities). Immunolabeling showed that some asynchronously lost NMJs were reinnervated by other motor units (N=4), confirming that vacated postsynaptic sites were not refractory to reinnervation in general.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 document the unexpected finding that motor units preferentially form heterologous rather than autologous connections. The quantitative data (2/21 autologous vs extensive heterologous reinnervation) and immunolabeling controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) support this conclusion. This finding contrasts with normal nerve injury responses.

result: The initial NMJ pool of surviving motor units gradually receded even though total motor unit size remained stable or increased due to heterologous expansions. Motor units are highly dynamic during disease progression, with specific branches either expanding or disassembling rather than being exclusively degenerating or compensating.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 synthesize the findings into a model of motor unit dynamism. This interpretation is well-supported by the imaging data showing simultaneous losses and gains within individual motor units. The conclusion challenges the dichotomous view of motor units as either degenerating or compensating.

result: Asynchronous NMJ dismantling tended to propagate from the first lost NMJ (multivariate GLM, interaction p<0.001). Adjacent denervation events (<300 μm) occurred preferentially within the next two sessions, while remote events (>300 μm) occurred exclusively three or more sessions later. This propagation pattern suggests that factors extrinsic to motor axons (local neuromuscular environment) interact with intrinsic axonal properties to shape NMJ loss patterns.
evaluation: Claims C53-C56 identify spatial-temporal propagation of denervation. The statistical analysis (GLM with p<0.001) on 37 events across 141 NMJs from 9 motor unit arbors provides strong support. The interpretation of extrinsic factor involvement (C56) is a reasonable inference from the propagation pattern, though the specific mechanisms remain speculative.

result: Single motor neurons initially lose NMJs asynchronously while contemporaneously expanding their axonal arbors to form new synaptic contacts in SOD1G37R mice. The resulting increase in axonal arbor size masks the underlying NMJ dismantlement, reconciling the 'dying-back hypothesis' with observed motor unit enlargement. NMJ denervation in ALS is a complex and dynamic process of continuous denervation and new innervation rather than a manifestation of sudden global motor neuron degeneration.
evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C93-C94, and C97 present the main conclusions synthesizing all findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive longitudinal imaging data showing asynchronous losses, contemporaneous sprouting, and the biphasic pattern of degeneration. The reconciliation of dying-back with motor unit enlargement is a significant conceptual advance.

result: NMJ denervation in a motor unit is initially slow, taking place over more than a month in SOD1G37R mice. This reveals a long time-window after the onset of NMJ loss during which motor neurons are not globally degenerating and preserve their capacity to reinnervate NMJs, representing a potential therapeutic window.
evaluation: Claims C60-C61 and C92 highlight the therapeutic implications. The temporal data (>1 month of asynchronous changes before global degeneration in 11/19 arbors) clearly demonstrates an extended window. The therapeutic interpretation (C92) is reasonable speculation supported by the data, though actual therapeutic efficacy would require additional studies.

result: The propagating pattern of denervation events and asynchronous changes within single motor units suggest that neuromuscular factors extrinsic to motor axons affect or contribute to NMJ loss in ALS. These factors would presumably interact with intrinsic vulnerability of axonal branches, with distal branches being more susceptible than proximal ones.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 and C95-C96 propose a mechanistic model involving both extrinsic and intrinsic factors. The propagation pattern (C53) and differential susceptibility by branch order (C44-C45) support this model. While the specific extrinsic factors remain unidentified, the inference of their involvement is reasonable from the spatial-temporal patterns observed.

result: Motor units are not segregated as either degenerating or compensating in ALS. Rather, a broad spectrum of motor unit phenotypes exists, with the majority continuously alternating between expansion and disassembly for weeks. Time-lapse analysis revealed that only some motor units underwent gains and losses in the same session.
evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C74 challenge previous models. The data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing 13/19 arbors with both losses and gains, though not always simultaneously, supports this conclusion. This finding contrasts with prior single-timepoint studies and highlights the value of longitudinal imaging.

result: The asynchronous branch-specific behavior observed contrasts with previous observations by Schaefer et al. (2005) in SOD1G93A mice. Several factors may explain this discrepancy: time-lapse analysis reveals that motor units often appear exclusively degenerating or compensating at single timepoints; fragmented branches indicating degeneration were seldom observed (9/38); and the present study focused exclusively on fast-fatigable motor units.
evaluation: Claims C72-C78 address apparent discrepancies with prior literature. The explanations provided are reasonable: single timepoint limitations (C74), low frequency of observing fragmented morphology (C75), and potential motor unit type differences (C76). However, the authors note that Pun et al. (2006) also found no compensatory reinnervation in the same muscle region, suggesting the discrepancy may not be fully resolved.

result: The pattern of motor unit changes in ALS is reminiscent of post-natal synapse elimination, where axonal branch elimination is also asynchronous and branch-specific. This resemblance suggests similar molecular mechanisms could be involved, potentially including branch-specific microtubule destabilization, as pharmacological microtubule stabilization is beneficial in ALS mice.
evaluation: Claims C79-C83 propose mechanistic parallels with developmental synapse elimination. While the phenomenological similarity is noted (C79), the inference of shared molecular mechanisms (C80, C83) is highly speculative. The citations support that microtubule destabilization occurs in development (C81) and that stabilization helps in ALS (C82), but direct evidence linking these processes is lacking.

result: Motor neurons failed to re-innervate their own lost NMJs despite preserving their capacity to sprout and form new synaptic contacts onto heterologous postsynaptic sites. This contrasts with normal axonal lesion responses where motor axons usually autologously reinnervate their original sites with great fidelity. Possible explanations include heterologous sprouts or molecular signals preventing original axon reinnervation, or that distal branches (where losses occur) are intrinsically less likely to form sprouts.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 identify an unexpected finding. The data clearly show low autologous reinnervation (2/21) despite high heterologous reinnervation (76/253). The contrast with normal nerve injury (C85) is well-established. The proposed explanations (C86-C87) are speculative but reasonable hypotheses for future investigation.

result: NMJs arising from distal branches in complex arbors are more susceptible than proximal ones at the single motor neuron level in ALS, consistent with previous results. These findings support the notion that larger axonal arborization size increases energetic load on neurons, making them more vulnerable to pathological insults. The constant dynamism and excessive motor unit expansions may further increase energetic load, adding to motor neuron stress during disease progression.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 are well-supported by the data (C44) and consistent with prior work (Tallon et al., 2016). The energetic load hypothesis is supported by citations (Le Masson et al., 2014; Pacelli et al., 2015). However, the speculation that motor unit dynamism increases energetic load (C90) is reasonable but lacks direct evidence.

result: In vivo imaging reveals a previously unsuspected dynamism at the NMJ in an animal model of ALS.
evaluation: Claim C91 is a summary statement well-supported by all the imaging data showing simultaneous losses and gains, propagation patterns, and the biphasic nature of degeneration. This represents a significant advance over prior single-timepoint studies.

result: The introduction establishes the context that NMJ loss is a key early pathological event in ALS occurring before symptom onset and motor neuron loss, with specific motor unit types affected sequentially. However, whether this reflects local branch-specific degeneration or global motor neuron dysfunction remains unclear, and local synaptic alterations occur early in ALS.
evaluation: Claims C1-C10 provide background context from prior literature. All claims are supported by appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the study but do not represent new findings from this work.

result: SOD1G37R mice are well known for their slow disease progression, making them an ideal model to follow single motor unit changes over time.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 justify the model choice. The slow progression of SOD1G37R mice is well-established (Boillée et al., 2006b; Lobsiger et al., 2009), and the inference that this makes them suitable for longitudinal imaging (C12) is reasonable and validated by the successful execution of the study.

result: Functional single motor unit recordings from ALS patients identify a majority of enlarged motor units and a subset of abnormally small motor units reflecting extensive NMJ dismantlement.
evaluation: Claim C59 cites prior clinical findings (Dengler et al., 1990; Schmied et al., 1999) that are consistent with the current study's findings. This represents appropriate contextualization of the results rather than a new finding.

result: Peripheral stabilization of NMJs and motor units represents an attractive therapeutic target in ALS, particularly given the accessibility of the neuromuscular system (no blood-brain barrier). Various mechanisms including chemo-repulsive molecules, trophic factors, NMJ stabilizing signals, and dysfunctional glial cells are of therapeutic interest.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 and C66-C69 discuss therapeutic implications. While the identification of a therapeutic window is supported by the data (C60-C61), the specific therapeutic strategies mentioned (C66-C69) are cited from prior work and represent speculation about future directions rather than tested interventions. The accessibility argument (C63) is valid but does not constitute evidence of therapeutic efficacy.
